q: Main social function of family
explanation: The family's social functions include reproduction (population replacement), status ascription and socialisation, so 'all of the above'.

notes.text: - **Primary functions (NextGen):** reproduction and rearing, **culture transmission**, home, **agent of socialisation**, **status ascription**, social control.

q: The single most important socializing agency in all forms of society
explanation: The family is the single most important socialising agency in every society.

notes.text: - **First and most important agency of socialisation:** the **family** (then school, peer group, community).

q: Duties in Modern Family
explanation: Many traditional duties of the family (education, care, production) have moved to schools, the state and markets, so the functions of the modern family are decreasing. Off-topic, moved to book 2 row 106.

notes.text: - **Family today** is no longer the main unit of production and has **lost many traditional functions** – both statements correct.

explanation: 'Socialisation is a process by which the individual is adapted to his social environment' is James Drever's definition (A Dictionary of Psychology). Moved to the family and socialisation row.

q: The process of personality development is completed in how many Stages according to Erikson.
explanation: Erik Erikson's psychosocial theory has eight stages, from trust vs mistrust (infancy) to integrity vs despair (old age).

q: The statuses of husbands and wives can be said in this way?
explanation: The statuses of husband and wife are functional (complementary) statuses, each defined by the role it plays in the family.

q: Who said that joint family is an extended kinship group in India?
explanation: Irawati Karve defined the joint family as a group living under one roof, eating from one hearth, holding property in common and related as a type of kindred, i.e. an extended kinship group.

notes.text: - **Karve's definition:** people under one roof, one hearth, common property, common worship, related as kindred – an **extended kinship group**; jointness = functional unity and obligations, may hold common property.

q: Author of the book 'Marriage and Family in India'?
explanation: Marriage and Family in India (1955) is by K.M. Kapadia, the pioneer of family studies in India.

q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of a joint family?
explanation: A joint family has co-residence, common property and common worship; private ownership of property is not its characteristic.

notes.text: - **Joint family:** **co-residence**, one hearth, **joint ownership of property**, **common worship**, pooled income; members are **kin** – private property and "unrelated members" are not features.

q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of a joint family?
options: All members living in one household
Members need not be related to each other
The entire property belongs to the family
key_text: Members need not be related to each other
explanation: Joint family members live in one household, hold property in common and pool income, and are related by kinship; 'members need not be related' is false.

notes.text: - **Joint family:** **co-residence**, one hearth, **joint ownership of property**, **common worship**, pooled income; members are **kin** – private property and "unrelated members" are not features.

q: In which year Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act introduced?
explanation: The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act was passed in 1956 with the Hindu Succession and Minority and Guardianship Acts.

q: Under Family Courts Act 1984, Family Courts can be set up by
explanation: Under the Family Courts Act, 1984 the State Government, after consulting the High Court, sets up family courts (mandatory in cities over one million).

q: A Nair family is called
explanation: A Nair matrilineal joint family is the tharavad (tharwad). Ghotul is the Muria youth dormitory; Nokna and Illam are distractors.

q: Which of the following is the main factor behind the disintegration of the joint family system in India?
explanation: Industrialisation and urbanisation (migration for jobs, wage work, small urban housing) are the main forces breaking up the joint family; laws, women's education and freedom are secondary factors.

q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of a modern family?
explanation: The modern family shows financial independence of members, decline of religious control and greater freedom for women; increased religious feeling is not its trait.

q: As per the child Marriage Act 2006, which of the following is not a crime
options: For an adult male to marry a minor child wife
To perform or help for child marriage in any way
To allow, encourage or fail to stop a child marriage (as a parent or guardian)
explanation: The PCMA 2006 punishes an adult male who marries a child (Sec. 9), anyone who performs or abets a child marriage (Sec. 10) and parents/guardians who promote it or fail to stop it (Sec. 11); merely taking part as a guest is the option the key treats as not a separate crime.

q: This act was the first legislative provision in India to provide consent for the performance of inter-caste marriages?
explanation: The Special (Civil/Native) Marriage Act, 1872 was the first law to permit civil, including inter-caste, marriage; the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 came much later (same question as Civil Services 'first legislative provision for inter-caste marriage').

q: The Hindu Marriage Act was enacted in the following year?
explanation: The Hindu Marriage Act was enacted in 1955 – the first codified Hindu marriage law after Independence.

q: After a landmark Judgement on Triple Talaq in 2017, which among the following methods of Which divorce practised in Muslim society was recently challenged in the Apex Court of India?
explanation: Talaq-e-Hasan, with talaq pronounced once a month over three months, was challenged in the Supreme Court after the 2017 triple talaq verdict. Talaq-e-Ahsan is a single pronouncement plus iddat and is not the one challenged.

notes.text: - **Talaq-e-Hasan:** talaq once a month over **three months**; challenged in the SC after the 2017 triple-talaq verdict; **Talaq-e-Ahsan** = a single pronouncement + iddat.

q: Muhammadan marriage is a
explanation: Muslim marriage (nikah) is a civil contract – an agreement – not a sacrament as Hindu marriage traditionally is.

notes.text: - **Muslim law:** marriage (Nikah) is a **contract**, solemnised by a **Kazi** (Kazis Act 1880) through a *nikahnama*; **Mehr** = the sum fixed at marriage and **payable to the bride** (prompt or on divorce/death); **khula** = divorce at the wife's instance by mutual consent.
- Hindu marriage = a **sacrament** (homa, panigrahana, saptapadi); Muslim marriage = a **contract**.

q: "Mutha" is one form of marriage, which can be observed in
explanation: Muta (Mutah) is the temporary contract marriage recognised among (Shia) Muslims.

notes.text: - **Muslim law:** marriage (Nikah) is a **contract**, solemnised by a **Kazi** (Kazis Act 1880) through a *nikahnama*; **Mehr** = the sum fixed at marriage and **payable to the bride** (prompt or on divorce/death); **khula** = divorce at the wife's instance by mutual consent.

q: Devara Nyaya Marriage is
options: Marriage with her deceased husband's brother
key_text: Marriage with her deceased husband's brother
explanation: Devara Nyayam is the Telugu name for levirate: a widow marries her deceased husband's brother. Marriage with a sister's daughter is menarikam.

notes.text: - **Levirate = husband's brother; Sororate = wife's sister** – both after the spouse's death.

q: Polygamy is this type of marriage
options: A woman having only one man as her husband
A woman marrying a man and his brother
explanation: Polygamy means having more than one spouse at a time; of the options only 'a woman marrying many men' (polyandry, a form of polygamy) describes plural marriage. B is monogamy; C (husband and his brother) is also polyandry but only its fraternal sub-type, so A is the better answer.

q: If a man marries more than one sister (Several Sisters) it is called this.
explanation: A man marrying several sisters is sororal polygyny; option C ('conjugal polygamy') is the translated rendering of that term. Levirate is marriage with a deceased husband's brother and endogamy is marriage within the group.

q: A woman is married to her husband's brother. This marriage is called
explanation: A woman married to her (deceased) husband's brother is levirate, called Devara Nyayam in Telugu; 'justice for wife and sister' is sororate.

notes.text: - **Levirate = husband's brother; Sororate = wife's sister** – both after the spouse's death.

q: Devara Nyaya is marriage of a man
options: Childless, with his dead brother's wife
key_text: Childless, with his dead brother's wife
explanation: Devara Nyayam (levirate) is a man's marriage with his dead brother's widow; marriage with the late wife's sister is sororate.

notes.text: - **Levirate = husband's brother; Sororate = wife's sister** – both after the spouse's death.

q: When the wife's husbands are brothers, then it is called as?
explanation:
Most books and keys: fraternal polyandry (A). Strictly: adelphic polyandry (B) is a synonym and equally correct.
When a woman's husbands are brothers it is fraternal polyandry (Toda). 'Adelphic polyandry' is only a synonym of the same thing; sororate and levirate concern a dead spouse's sibling.

q: Once a man marries a woman once it is
explanation: One man married to one woman is monogamy; polygamy and polyandry involve more than one spouse.

q: What is the name of inter caste marriage if a man of lower caste marries a woman of higher caste?
explanation: A lower-caste man marrying a higher-caste woman is pratiloma (hypogamy) and was condemned; anuloma is a higher-caste man with a lower-caste woman.

notes.text: - **⚠ Trap:** anuloma ≠ pratiloma – in both terms the direction is the **woman's** marriage relative to her own caste.

q: A marriage within the same caste is thus called
explanation: Marriage within one's own caste is endogamy (Telugu antar-vivaham), which the translated paper renders as 'intermarriage'; 'extramarriage' stands for exogamy.

q: Recently the Delhi High Court has upheld the constitutional validity of a provision of the Hindu Marriage Act which 'prohibits marriage between people who are related to each other through ancestors from their parent's side unless their customs allow them to do so'. The said provision was mentioned in which Section of the Hindu Marriage Act?
explanation: Section 5(v) of the Hindu Marriage Act bars marriage between sapindas unless custom permits; the Delhi High Court upheld it in 2024. 5(iv) is prohibited degrees, 12 voidable marriages, 13 divorce.

notes.text: - **Sec. 5(iv)** bars prohibited degrees; **Sec. 5(v)** bars **sapinda** marriage – both unless **custom** allows.
- **Delhi High Court (Jan 2024)** upheld **Sec. 5(v)** (sapinda bar).

q: A marriage ceremony between a high caste girl and a low caste boy is called
explanation: A high-caste girl marrying a low-caste boy is pratiloma marriage (condemned); anuloma is the reverse (high-caste man, low-caste woman).

notes.text: - **⚠ Trap:** anuloma ≠ pratiloma – in both terms the direction is the **woman's** marriage relative to her own caste.

q: Marriage of a high caste girl to a low caste boy is called
explanation: A high-caste girl marrying a low-caste boy is pratiloma (hypogamy); anuloma is a high-caste man with a low-caste woman, and endogamy/exogamy are rules about the group.

notes.text: - **⚠ Trap:** anuloma ≠ pratiloma – in both terms the direction is the **woman's** marriage relative to her own caste.

q: Hypogamy marriage means a marriage between:
options: A man of high caste and a woman of low caste
A man and a woman of high caste
A woman of high caste and a man of low caste
key_text: A woman of high caste and a man of low caste
explanation: Hypogamy is a woman of higher caste marrying a man of lower caste (pratiloma); hypergamy (anuloma) is a higher-caste man with a lower-caste woman.

q: Which of the following was the custom practised during the ancient period that allows married women to cohabit with a designated male for the sole purpose of procreating a child if her husband was impotent or had died?
explanation: Niyoga is the ancient custom in which a wife cohabits with a designated man to bear a child when her husband is impotent or dead; the other options are not names of this custom.

q: A consensual and informal relationship practised in accordance to matrilineal laws of Kerala that prevailed among Namboothiris and Nairs is known as:
explanation: Sambandham was the consensual, informal union of Namboothiris and Nairs under Kerala's matrilineal system.

q: Marriage by purchase of bride was known as
explanation: Marriage by purchase of the bride, with the groom's family paying a bride price, is the Asura form (option 'Asara' is a misprint). Paisacha is by deceit, Rakshasa by abduction, Prajapatya is an approved form.

q: Divorce occurs when
options: When husband and wife decide to live separately
When both spouses inform their parents
When the society believes that their marriage bond is broken
When the marriage is annulled by the court
key_text: When the marriage is annulled by the court
explanation: Divorce is the legal dissolution of a marriage by a court (W.P. Scott: an institutionalised arrangement for terminating the marriage); spouses merely deciding to live apart is separation, not divorce.

notes.text: - **Divorce** = the **legal dissolution of a marriage by a court**; **W.P. Scott**: "an institutionalised arrangement for terminating the marriage relationship and allowing each partner the right to remarry". Living apart is only separation.

q: In May 2023, the Supreme Court said that "it can exercise its powers under Article ___ of the constitution to grant divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of a marriage" even if one of the parties opposes it.
explanation: In May 2023 (Shilpa Sailesh) the Supreme Court held it can use Article 142(1) to grant divorce on irretrievable breakdown of marriage even if one party opposes.

notes.text: - **Irretrievable breakdown** is not an HMA ground; **May 2023 (Shilpa Sailesh)**: the SC can dissolve such a marriage under **Art. 142(1)** even if one party opposes.

q: Relatives by marriage are called
explanation: Relatives by marriage are affinal relatives (affines); consanguineous relatives are blood kin, and tertiary relatives are a degree of kinship. The options are a translation of 'affinal'.

q: Kinship by marriage is called
explanation: Kinship by marriage is affinal kinship, rendered here as 'matrimonial kinship'; consanguinity is kinship by blood.

q: It is said that marriage is a source of kinship. Who said this?
explanation: The printed key credits Westermarck (History of Human Marriage) with the view that marriage is a source of kinship; Radcliffe-Brown defined kinship as dynamic relations regulated by social usage.

notes.text: - **Marriage creates kinship** (Westermarck, APPSC 2000 key): when two people marry they become kin to one another.

q: When a person dies, his immovable property is transferred from one person to another. This is
explanation: Transfer of a dead person's property to heirs is inheritance; adoption is taking another's child as one's own.

notes.text: - **Inheritance** = transfer of property (immovable) from a dead person to heirs.

q: In a patriarchal society, the principle that the mother's brother plays the most important and ritualistic social role is called this.
explanation: In a patrilineal (patriarchal) society the ritual and social role of the mother's brother reflects complementary filiation (Meyer Fortes) – the tie with the mother's kin; consanguinity is mere blood relationship. Same item as the 'complementary filiations' question (printed key here: A).

q: Where more respect is given to the father's female sibling than the mother, such a relationship is called?
explanation: Special respect for the father's sister over the mother is amitate (rendered 'patriarchal relationship'); avunculate concerns the maternal uncle, couvade the husband's pregnancy rites, teknonymy naming through a child.

q: Cognatic kinship system is
explanation: Cognatic kinship means bilateral descent – traced equally through father and mother.

q: The practice of the newly married couple living with the wife's family after marriage is known as
explanation: A couple living with the wife's family after marriage follows matrilocal residence; with the husband's family is patrilocal, with the maternal uncle avunculocal (matula-sthanika).

q: Matrilineal family system belongs to them.
explanation: The Nairs follow the matrilineal tharavad system; Namboodiris, Muslims (mainland) and Coorgs are patrilineal.

notes.text: - Matrilineal communities: **Nairs** (Kerala), **Khasis** and **Garos** (Meghalaya); "pro-matriarchal" pair asked: **Nairs and Khasis**.
- **⚠ Trap:** Namboodiris are patrilineal Brahmins (they joined Nair women only in **sambandham**); Coorgs are patrilineal.

explanation: Marriage of a man with his elder sister's daughter is uncle–niece marriage, called menarikam in Telugu (here 'Paitruka Menarikam'); anuloma and pratiloma are inter-caste marriages.

q: Cross cousin marriage is between a man and one of the following?

explanation: A cross-cousin is the child of the mother's brother or the father's sister, so cross-cousin marriage is with the mother's brother's daughter; father's brother's daughter is a parallel cousin.

notes.text: - **Family scenario (APPSC 2025):** Krishna (son) – Jyothi (sister's daughter) = **consanguineous**; spouses and in-laws = affinal.

q: Jajmani system is a
explanation: The jajmani system is at once economic (exchange of services for grain), political (patron dominance) and socio-cultural/ritual, so 'all of the above'.

notes.text: - **Jajmani system** = a **socio-economic and ritual** arrangement in which one caste secures the services of another; everyone works for a family or group to which he is **hereditarily** linked – so it is at once economic, political and socio-cultural.

q: Jajmani system is
explanation: Jajmani ties are hereditary: a family serves the same patron family generation after generation.

notes.text: - **Jajmani system** = a **socio-economic and ritual** arrangement in which one caste secures the services of another; everyone works for a family or group to which he is **hereditarily** linked – so it is at once economic, political and socio-cultural.
- **Jajman** = the **landholding** patron caste; **kamin** = the castes rendering hereditary services; paid in kind (grain share) at harvest.

q: Tribal economic relations mainly depended on this
explanation: Tribal economic relations depended mainly on barter; the jajmani system links castes in a village, not tribes (printed key: jajmani).

notes.text: - **⚠ Trap:** jajmani is a **caste-village** system; economic exchange **between tribes** is mainly **barter**.

q: The mutual dependence of castes is known as this.
explanation: The hereditary interdependence of castes – service castes (kamin) serving landholding patrons (jajman) – is the jajmani system; 'mutual unity' is not a sociological term.

notes.text: - **Jajmani system** = a **socio-economic and ritual** arrangement in which one caste secures the services of another; everyone works for a family or group to which he is **hereditarily** linked – so it is at once economic, political and socio-cultural.

- Features: **functional interdependence** of castes, **hereditary** ties, **inequality** of status between groups; critics (Beidelman) call it exploitative, but "feudalism" is not a defining feature.

q: Who used the term 'untouchable' for the scheduled castes for the first time?

q: Who holds the view that caste is a broad kinship group?
explanation: Irawati Karve (Hindu Society: An Interpretation, 1961) saw the jati as an extended kin group: endogamous, limited to a linguistic region and usually with a hereditary occupation. Ghurye stressed six structural features and Risley race (printed key: G.S. Ghurye).

q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of caste?
explanation: Caste features are endogamy ('inter-marriage' = antar-vivaha, marriage within), hereditary occupation and commensal (meal) rules; complexion is not a feature of caste. Off-topic (society), moved.

notes.text: - **Ghurye** (*Caste and Race in India*, **1932**), **six features**: segmental division; hierarchy; restrictions on feeding and social intercourse; civil and religious disabilities and privileges; **lack of free choice of occupation**; restrictions on marriage (endogamy).
